title: drawing through a life rupture
content:
life from my sketchbook

this past December, due to a residency permit rejection, I had to leave my life in Istanbul and enter a year of uncertainty and suspension — literally, my Hanged Man year — as I try to figure out what’s next.

this year of liminal floating time felt like the perfect opportunity to arrive and ground, again, in an ongoing sketchbook practice.

here are the series of pages from my sketchbook in the transition weeks, right after leaving — when I traveled to Paris and New York, before landing at my parents’ in North Carolina. with each movement, I drew the images in my head, the visuals that stayed with me, and how I felt.

   

Istanbul, a swirling whirlpool


December 8th, a few days before leaving

I remember feeling like I weighed 1000 tons when I drew this image. I was sitting at my desk, looking out of my window, and I just drew what I saw — the Bosphorus strait, heavy winter clouds, the silhouette of a mosque. but, drawing what I saw didn’t capture how I felt — so I added what I imagined: the whirlpool, the tiny boat, the woman (me) laying there, waiting for time to carry me away, inevitably.

I was on my period, hence the red. after adding my imaginary elements to make this image feel no longer calm, but tumultous — then I felt better, and could step away.

   

Paris, mysterious unreal days

December 11-15

after I left Istanbul, I flew to Paris a few days for a weekend tango event. I did not really want to go, but by the time I was there, it felt like Paris had enveloped me completely, like a foggy, surrealist dream. I was staying in an unexpectedly tiny, shoebox airbnb, where I slept at 3 or 4 or 5 am every night, and woke up to totalizing grey skies. I never saw another person in the entire building, but I heard them clearly, through the walls. those days,

the first morning, I walked to Père Lachaise Cemetery, and communed with the dead. I walked through old neighborhoods I had remembered from 2020, when I started my nomadic life by leaving NYC, and flying to Paris.

I sat in the neon glow of a orb light and felt myself wanting to disappear. I noticed an urge to delete my past, and start over. in this city, or any city.

in those days, combined with dancing tango, I felt very untethered to reality. what was truly real, and what was a dream?

*

   

*

New York, familiar verticals

December 15-24

I actually didn’t draw those Paris pages until I was already in New York. I spent most subway rides opening my sketchbook, trying to capture the essence of my Paris experience — as if trying to recall a memory, or a faint dream. nobody cares what you do in NYC, so I was very unself-conscious.

(that is, until a man got up and asked to see what I was drawing, which I reluctantly showed him, then asked to see the previous page, which I reluctantly showed him, then started flipping through my sketchbook of his own accord, while I was a bit startled and shocked, and embarrassed about, as onlookers glanced, then took out his phone to show me his pencil portraits, which I nodded at politely, then hurried out, at the next stop. I felt over-exposed, from just trying to be polite).

*

I drew the subway, because I looked at it everyday. I started drawing a vertical view of midtown skyscrapers, at night. I drew a quick sketch of myself, the feeling of floating in the water, surrendering or dead or sleeping. (or, the same position as end of the menstrual cycle mood, though it wasn’t that time for me).

New York was full of vertical lines and dirty efficiency, but I felt like bitter molasses — as if drugged and slow and yet, life felt like it was glittering with a violence and thrill to it.

    

I didn’t “finish” these New York sketches. not really. but I didn’t feel very interested in drawing them anymore, so I let them go.

on Christmas Day, I took a 10 hour Amtrak train to North Carolina, where I landed at my parents’ place. I drew those first days and weeks. I’ll post those pages soon.

*

drawing life as witnessing

I’ve been metabolizing my life through art for as long as I can remember — for years, I kept a mood diary of extreme feelings. I kept these visual diaries for the first few months of 2025. I drew fragments here and there, scattered through my 10 years of archives.

but re-starting a sketchbook practice feels different this time — possibly because the stakes of my life feel higher. more dramatic. no matter what happens outside, there is such comfort in knowing that I can return here, to these pages — and allow myself to witness what I lived through, both what I saw and what I observed, and the truth of what I felt. it feels like refuge and tenderness — even (or especially), when things feel hard.
